TRUST DECANTING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · The Pat Morgan Living Trust

BACKGROUND INFORMATION — TRUST DECANTING
I, Jordan Lee, am serving, or have been asked to serve, as trustee of The Pat Morgan Living Trust, executed June 1, 2015 (referred to in this information sheet as the "first trust"). This information sheet describes California's statutory trust decanting framework, the Uniform Trust Decanting Act (Probate Code § 19501 et seq.), as background in connection with a potential distribution of principal from The Pat Morgan Living Trust to a proposed second trust, The Pat Morgan 2026 Trust. This information sheet is not itself an exercise of the decanting power described in this document, is not the signed writing that Probate Code § 19510 requires to exercise that power, and is not the notice that Probate Code § 19507 requires before that power is exercised. Preparing, reviewing, or signing this information sheet does not distribute any property out of The Pat Morgan Living Trust, does not modify The Pat Morgan Living Trust's terms, and does not satisfy Jordan Lee's notice obligation, if any, in connection with The Pat Morgan Living Trust or any other trust. Only an actual signed writing that satisfies § 19510, preceded (or accompanied, as § 19507 allows in limited circumstances) by notice that satisfies § 19507 or a signed waiver of that notice period, does that.

WHAT 'DECANTING' MEANS UNDER CALIFORNIA'S UNIFORM TRUST DECANTING ACT
California's Uniform Trust Decanting Act, enacted in 2018 and codified at Probate Code §§ 19501-19530, defines the 'decanting power' as the power of an authorized fiduciary to distribute property of a 'first trust' to one or more 'second trusts,' or to modify the terms of the first trust. A 'first trust' is a trust over which an authorized fiduciary may exercise the decanting power -- potentially The Pat Morgan Living Trust -- and a 'second trust' is either the first trust itself after modification under the Act, or a separate trust to which a distribution of property from the first trust is or may be made, such as a proposed The Pat Morgan 2026 Trust. Decanting under this Act is therefore a mechanism a trustee (or certain other fiduciaries) can use, not one a settlor uses directly; it operates by the fiduciary distributing or redirecting trust principal, or reshaping the first trust's own terms, rather than by the settlor amending or restating the instrument.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Decanting power” or “the decanting power” means the power of an authorized fiduciary under this part to distribute property of a first trust to one or more second trusts or to modify the terms of the first trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19502(j) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of the 'decanting power' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19502.)
  "“First trust” means a trust over which an authorized fiduciary may exercise the decanting power."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19502(l) (California Legislative Information text), the definition of a 'first trust' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19502.)
  "“Second trust” means either of the following:(1) A first trust after modification under this part.(2) A trust to which a distribution of property from a first trust is or may be made under this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19502(v) (California Legislative Information text), the definition of a 'second trust' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19502.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's decanting framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust; other states that have adopted the Uniform Trust Decanting Act, or that use their own decanting statutes, can differ from California's version in scope and detail, and this document addresses California's enactment only. This clause cites three different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 19502 (subdivisions (j), (l), and (v)); no single subdivision is quoted more than once in this clause, and all three subdivisions come from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times. This document does not determine whether any specific trust is, in fact, a 'first trust' over which any specific person may exercise the decanting power, or whether a specific proposed new trust would qualify as a 'second trust' under the Act -- addressed further, as to threshold eligibility, in a separate clause of this document.

WHO MAY EXERCISE THE DECANTING POWER, AND WHAT KIND OF TRUST THE ACT APPLIES TO
The Act's threshold requirement is built into its definition of who counts as an 'authorized fiduciary' able to exercise the decanting power at all: principally, a trustee or other fiduciary, other than a settlor, that already has discretion to distribute or direct a trustee to distribute part or all of the principal of the first trust to one or more current beneficiaries. Without that pre-existing discretion to distribute principal, a trustee is not an 'authorized fiduciary' under this Act, and the decanting power described in this document is not available to that trustee on that basis. Separately, the Act's own scope provision limits which trusts it reaches in the first place: except in limited circumstances, it applies to an express trust that is irrevocable, or that is revocable by the settlor only with the consent of the trustee or a person holding an adverse interest. A trust the settlor alone can still revoke or amend outright is accordingly outside the scope of this Act as described here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Authorized fiduciary” means any of the following:(1) A trustee or other fiduciary, other than a settlor, that has discretion to distribute or direct a trustee to distribute part or all of the principal of the first trust to one or more current beneficiaries."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19502(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the threshold discretion-to-distribute-principal requirement for an 'authorized fiduciary' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19502.)
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), this part applies to an express trust that is irrevocable or revocable by the settlor only with the consent of the trustee or a person holding an adverse interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19503(a) (California Legislative Information text), the scope of the Act: irrevocable trusts, or trusts revocable only with the trustee's or an adverse party's consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19503.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's decanting framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine whether any specific trustee actually holds the principal-distribution discretion the Act requires to qualify as an 'authorized fiduciary' of a specific trust, or whether a specific trust is, in fact, irrevocable or revocable only with the trustee's or an adverse party's consent -- those are fact- and instrument-specific questions this document does not resolve. This clause cites two different statutory sections, § 19502(c)(1) and § 19503(a); both come from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times. Separately, this corpus's own Trust Amendment document addresses a different statutory mechanism -- a settlor's own power under Probate Code § 15402 to modify a trust that is still revocable by that settlor -- which is why § 19503(a)'s scope language matters here: the Act described in this document is generally the mechanism available once a trust is no longer one the settlor alone can simply amend, not an alternative to that simpler amendment power for a trust that still is.

'EXPANDED' VERSUS 'LIMITED' DISTRIBUTIVE DISCRETION, AND WHY THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS
California's Act draws a distinction between two kinds of principal-distribution discretion a trustee may hold, and ties different decanting rules to each. 'Expanded distributive discretion' means a discretionary power of distribution that is not limited to an ascertainable standard or a reasonably definite standard -- broadly, discretion beyond a fixed standard such as a beneficiary's health, education, support, or maintenance. An authorized fiduciary with expanded distributive discretion over a first trust's principal may exercise the decanting power over that principal, subject to specific limits described elsewhere in this document. 'Limited distributive discretion,' by contrast, means a discretionary power of distribution that is limited to an ascertainable standard or a reasonably definite standard. A fiduciary with only limited distributive discretion may still exercise the decanting power over the first trust's principal, but under a different and more restrictive rule: the second trust or trusts, taken together, must grant each beneficiary of the first trust beneficial interests that are 'substantially similar' to that beneficiary's beneficial interests in the first trust, meaning no material change in those interests except as the statute itself allows.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Expanded distributive discretion” means a discretionary power of distribution that is not limited to an ascertainable standard or a reasonably definite standard."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19502(k) (California Legislative Information text), the definition of 'expanded distributive discretion' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19502.)
  "(b) Subject to subdivision (c) and Section 19514, an authorized fiduciary that has expanded distributive discretion over the principal of a first trust for the benefit of one or more current beneficiaries may exercise the decanting power over the principal of the first trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19511(b) (California Legislative Information text), an authorized fiduciary's authority to decant principal held under expanded distributive discretion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19511.)
  "(a) For purposes of this section, “limited distributive discretion” means a discretionary power of distribution that is limited to an ascertainable standard or a reasonably definite standard."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19512(a) (California Legislative Information text), the definition of 'limited distributive discretion' for purposes of § 19512 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19512.)
  "(c) Under this section and subject to Section 19514, a second trust may be created or administered under the law of any jurisdiction. Under this section, the second trusts, in the aggregate, shall grant each beneficiary of the first trust beneficial interests which are substantially similar to the beneficial interests of the beneficiary in the first trust. For purposes of this subdivision, “substantially similar” means that there is no material change in a beneficiary’s beneficial interests, except as provided in subdivision (d)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19512(c) (California Legislative Information text), the substantially-similar-interests requirement that applies to decanting under limited distributive discretion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19512.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's Act specifically draws this distinction -- not an assumption that California's version matches every other state's decanting statute, or the model Uniform Trust Decanting Act, on this point; the presence and precise scope of an expanded/limited-discretion distinction can vary by state, and this document addresses California's current text only. This clause cites four different statutory sections -- § 19502(k) (defining 'expanded distributive discretion'), § 19511(b) (the expanded-discretion authority to decant), § 19512(a) (defining 'limited distributive discretion' for purposes of that section), and § 19512(c) (the substantially-similar requirement) -- fetched as part of the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times. This clause does not itself catalog every specific change a second trust may or may not make under either form of discretion -- that is addressed, for the expanded-discretion case, in a separate clause of this document; this document does not separately catalog every specific change (beyond the substantially-similar standard) available or unavailable under limited distributive discretion.

NOTICE BEFORE DECANTING, THE RIGHT TO OBJECT, AND WHY COURT APPROVAL IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY REQUIRED
An authorized fiduciary may exercise the decanting power without the consent of any person and without court approval, so long as the fiduciary complies with the Act's own requirements -- chiefly, advance notice. Except in limited circumstances, the fiduciary must give notice of the intended exercise of the decanting power not later than 60 days before the exercise to each settlor of the first trust then living or in existence, each qualified beneficiary of the first trust, each holder of a presently exercisable power of appointment over any part of the first trust, each person who currently has the right to remove or replace the authorized fiduciary, each other fiduciary of the first trust, each fiduciary of the second trust, and the Attorney General if the first trust holds certain charitable interests. Separately, the Act defines a 'notice period' for this purpose as beginning on the day notice is given and ending 59 days after that day, and requires the notice itself to include a specific warning, in boldface type, that a recipient who does not bring a court action to contest the proposed decanting within 59 days of the notice will lose the right to contest it. Receiving notice does not prevent a person from later applying to court: on application by an authorized fiduciary, a person entitled to notice, a beneficiary, or (as to a charitable interest) the Attorney General, a court may provide instructions on whether a proposed exercise is permitted, appoint a special fiduciary, approve an exercise of the decanting power, or grant other relief the Act separately describes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) An authorized fiduciary may exercise the decanting power without the consent of any person and without court approval in compliance with this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19507(b) (California Legislative Information text), an authorized fiduciary may decant without any person's consent and without court approval (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19507.)
  "(a) In this section, a notice period begins on the day notice is given under subdivision (c) and ends 59 days after the day notice is given."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19507(a) (California Legislative Information text), the definition of the 59-day 'notice period' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19507.)
  "(c) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (h), an authorized fiduciary shall give notice of the intended exercise of the decanting power not later than 60 days before the exercise to all of the following:(1) Each settlor of the first trust, if living or then in existence.(2) Each qualified beneficiary of the first trust.(3) Each holder of a presently exercisable power of appointment over any part or all of the first trust.(4) Each person that currently has the right to remove or replace the authorized fiduciary.(5) Each other fiduciary of the first trust.(6) Each fiduciary of the second trust.(7) The Attorney General, if subdivision (b) of Section 19514 applies."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19507(c) (California Legislative Information text), who must receive notice, and the 60-day advance-notice deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19507.)
  "(5) A warning, set out in a separate paragraph in not less than 10-point bold type, or a reasonable equivalent thereof, that states the following:“If you do not bring a court action to contest the proposed trust decanting (the proposed changes to the trust) within 59 days of this notice, you will lose your right to contest the decanting.”"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19507(g)(5) (California Legislative Information text), the required boldface warning of the 59-day contest deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19507.)
  "(a) On application of an authorized fiduciary, a person entitled to notice under subdivision (c) of Section 19507, a beneficiary, or, with respect to a charitable interest, the Attorney General or other person that has standing to enforce the charitable interest, the court may do any of the following:(1) Provide instructions to the authorized fiduciary regarding whether a proposed exercise of the decanting power is permitted under this part and is consistent with the fiduciary duties of the authorized fiduciary.(2) Appoint a special fiduciary and authorize the special fiduciary to determine whether the decanting power should be exercised under this part and to exercise the decanting power.(3) Approve an exercise of the decanting power."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19509(a) (California Legislative Information text), who may apply to court, and the relief a court may order regarding a decanting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19509.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's decanting notice framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust; notice periods and required contents vary across states that have adopted versions of the Uniform Trust Decanting Act. This document is informational: it does not itself constitute or serve the notice this section describes, and preparing it does not start, toll, or satisfy the 60-day notice deadline for any specific trust -- only an actual, compliant notice does that. This corrects a natural but imprecise assumption: the statute does not set a single symmetrical '60-day notice period.' The required advance notice must be given at least 60 days before the exercise, but the defined 'notice period' itself runs only 59 days from the day notice is given, and the required contest warning likewise refers to 59 days, not 60 -- so the advance-notice figure and the contest-window figure described in this clause are not the same number. This clause cites five different subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 19507 (subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (g)(5)), plus a separate section, § 19509(a); all come from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times. Section 19507 shows a 2023 amendment (effective January 1, 2024) in the fetched text, confirming this is the current, operative version rather than the statute's original 2019 text. This document does not address several related, narrower rules this research did not fully develop into their own clauses -- among them, that certain other actions under the Act (such as increasing an authorized fiduciary's own compensation, or modifying who may remove or replace the fiduciary) require either beneficiary consent or court approval even though the general decanting exercise described in this clause does not.

WHAT AN AUTHORIZED FIDUCIARY WITH EXPANDED DISCRETION CANNOT DO TO A BENEFICIARY'S INTEREST
Even where an authorized fiduciary holds expanded distributive discretion sufficient to exercise the decanting power, the Act places specific limits on what the resulting second trust may do. In an exercise of the decanting power under this expanded-discretion authority, a second trust may not include as a current beneficiary a person who is not already a current beneficiary of the first trust (except as the statute separately allows), may not include as a presumptive remainder or successor beneficiary a person who does not already hold one of those categories of interest in the first trust (subject to the same exception), and may not reduce or eliminate a 'vested interest' -- a term the Act itself defines to include, among other things, a current and noncontingent right to a mandatory distribution of income or a set dollar amount or percentage, and a presently exercisable general power of appointment. This is a narrower, more specific protection than a generic rule against reducing 'a beneficiary's interest' in the abstract: it turns on whether the particular interest at stake qualifies as a current beneficiary interest, a presumptive remainder or successor interest, or a statutorily defined vested interest, and it operates differently from the separate 'substantially similar' protection that applies instead when a fiduciary is decanting under limited, rather than expanded, distributive discretion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(c) Subject to Section 19513, in an exercise of the decanting power under this section, a second trust may not do any of the following:(1) Include as a current beneficiary a person that is not a current beneficiary of the first trust, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (d).(2) Include as a presumptive remainder beneficiary or successor beneficiary a person that is not a current beneficiary, presumptive remainder beneficiary, or successor beneficiary of the first trust, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (d).(3) Reduce or eliminate a vested interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19511(c) (California Legislative Information text), the restrictions on adding beneficiaries and reducing or eliminating a vested interest, under expanded distributive discretion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19511.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's specific beneficiary protections under this Act -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, or about how any specific first trust's beneficiaries or interests should be categorized under this statute. This corrects a natural but imprecise assumption from a generic description of decanting statutes: California's statute does not flatly bar 'adding a new beneficiary' in every sense, and it does not use a single undifferentiated concept of 'a beneficiary's fixed income interest.' The restriction in subdivision (c) is limited to adding a person as a current beneficiary, or as a presumptive remainder or successor beneficiary, who does not already hold an equivalent category of interest in the first trust (itself subject to an exception in subdivision (d), which this document does not independently quote or address, for new or modified powers of appointment in favor of existing beneficiaries), and the protection against reduction turns on the statute's own defined term 'vested interest' -- a term this document does not exhaustively quote in full -- rather than on every fixed or scheduled payment a beneficiary might expect. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 19511(c); no additional independent source was sought for this, and it was fetched as part of the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) described in this document's other clauses, twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times.

PROTECTIONS FOR TAX-SENSITIVE PROVISIONS AND CHARITABLE INTERESTS
The Act separately restricts decanting where a first trust holds a charitable interest or property whose tax treatment depends on specific terms. If a first trust contains a charitable interest, the second trust or trusts may not diminish that charitable interest, may not diminish the interest of an identified charitable organization that holds it, may not alter any charitable purpose stated in the first trust instrument, and may not alter any condition or restriction related to that charitable interest. Independently, a set of tax-qualification protections applies across a list of specific tax provisions the statute itself enumerates -- for example, if a first trust contains property that qualified, or would have qualified, for a marital deduction for gift or estate tax purposes, the second trust instrument may not include or omit a term that would have prevented that qualification, or reduced the deduction, under the same provision that let the original transfer qualify. The statute applies a parallel rule to several other tax-sensitive attributes it separately lists, including charitable-deduction qualification, the gift-tax annual exclusion, S-corporation shareholder eligibility, generation-skipping-transfer zero-inclusion-ratio status, and minimum-distribution treatment of retirement-plan property; the statute also gives a settlor, specifically, the right to object in a signed writing during the notice period where decanting would change whether the settlor retains the power to cause a trust to cease being a 'grantor trust' for income tax purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(c) If a first trust contains a charitable interest, the second trust or trusts may not do any of the following:(1) Diminish the charitable interest.(2) Diminish the interest of an identified charitable organization that holds the charitable interest.(3) Alter any charitable purpose stated in the first trust instrument.(4) Alter any condition or restriction related to the charitable interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19514(c) (California Legislative Information text), the restrictions on decanting a first trust that contains a charitable interest (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19514.)
  "(1) If a first trust contains property that qualified, or would have qualified but for provisions of this part other than this section, for a marital deduction for purposes of the gift or estate tax under the Internal Revenue Code or a state gift, estate, or inheritance tax, the second trust instrument shall not include or omit any term that, if included in or omitted from the trust instrument for the trust to which the property was transferred, would have prevented the transfer from qualifying for the deduction, or would have reduced the amount of the deduction, under the same provisions of the Internal Revenue Code or state law under which the transfer qualified."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19519(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), preservation of marital-deduction qualification as a representative tax-sensitive limitation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19519.)
  "(10) An authorized fiduciary may not exercise the decanting power if a settlor objects in a signed writing delivered to the fiduciary within the notice period and either of the following conditions is satisfied:(A) The first trust and a second trust are both grantor trusts, in whole or in part, the first trust grants the settlor or another person the power to cause the first trust to cease to be a grantor trust, and the second trust does not grant an equivalent power to the settlor or other person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 19519(b)(10) (California Legislative Information text), a settlor's right to object to a decanting that would change grantor-trust status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=19519.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's decanting protections for charitable interests and tax-sensitive provisions -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination that any specific trust actually holds a charitable interest or actually qualified for any specific tax benefit. This document quotes only two of the statute's tax-sensitive protections directly -- the charitable-interest restrictions in § 19514(c), and the marital-deduction protection in § 19519(b)(1) -- as representative examples of a considerably longer enumerated list in § 19519(b) that this document does not quote in full; the settlor's grantor-trust objection right described in this clause's body is drawn from § 19519(b)(10)(A), quoted below, which is one specific condition among the several that subdivision addresses, not the whole of it. This clause cites three different statutory sections -- § 19514(c), § 19519(b)(1), and § 19519(b)(10) -- all fetched as part of the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) described in this document's other clauses, twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times. This document does not independently verify the underlying federal tax rules (marital deduction, grantor trust status, or otherwise) that these state-law protections are designed to preserve; it addresses only what California's decanting statute itself requires or forbids in a second trust instrument.

SIGNATURE AND RECORD BLOCK — TRUST DECANTING INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at San Francisco, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee, as trustee of The Pat Morgan Living Trust: ☐ _________________________

It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete an exercise of the decanting power, and preparing or signing it does not satisfy the written-instrument requirement of Probate Code § 19510, the notice requirement of Probate Code § 19507, or any fiduciary duty Jordan Lee owes as trustee of The Pat Morgan Living Trust; only an actual exercise of the decanting power, carried out in the manner and within the time this document describes, does that.]

expectedJSON.body: California's Act draws a distinction between two kinds of principal-distribution discretion a trustee may hold, and ties different decanting rules to each. 'Expanded distributive discretion' means a discretionary power of distribution that is not limited to an ascertainable standard or a reasonably definite standard -- broadly, discretion beyond a fixed standard such as a beneficiary's health, education, support, or maintenance. An authorized fiduciary with expanded distributive discretion over a first trust's principal may exercise the decanting power over that principal, subject to specific limits described elsewhere in this document. 'Limited distributive discretion,' by contrast, means a discretionary power of distribution that is limited to an ascertainable standard or a reasonably definite standard. A fiduciary with only limited distributive discretion may still exercise the decanting power over the first trust's principal, but under a different and more restrictive rule: the second trust or trusts, taken together, must grant each beneficiary of the first trust beneficial interests that are 'substantially similar' to that beneficiary's beneficial interests in the first trust, meaning no material change in those interests except as the statute itself allows.

For purposes of this subdivision, “substantially similar” means that there is no material change in a beneficiary’s beneficial interests, except as provided in subdivision (d).

expectedJSON.body: An authorized fiduciary may exercise the decanting power without the consent of any person and without court approval, so long as the fiduciary complies with the Act's own requirements -- chiefly, advance notice. Except in limited circumstances, the fiduciary must give notice of the intended exercise of the decanting power not later than 60 days before the exercise to each settlor of the first trust then living or in existence, each qualified beneficiary of the first trust, each holder of a presently exercisable power of appointment over any part of the first trust, each person who currently has the right to remove or replace the authorized fiduciary, each other fiduciary of the first trust, each fiduciary of the second trust, and the Attorney General if the first trust holds certain charitable interests. Separately, the Act defines a 'notice period' for this purpose as beginning on the day notice is given and ending 59 days after that day, and requires the notice itself to include a specific warning, in boldface type, that a recipient who does not bring a court action to contest the proposed decanting within 59 days of the notice will lose the right to contest it. Receiving notice does not prevent a person from later applying to court: on application by an authorized fiduciary, a person entitled to notice, a beneficiary, or (as to a charitable interest) the Attorney General, a court may provide instructions on whether a proposed exercise is permitted, appoint a special fiduciary, approve an exercise of the decanting power, or grant other relief the Act separately describes.

This document is informational: it does not itself constitute or serve the notice this section describes, and preparing it does not start, toll, or satisfy the 60-day notice deadline for any specific trust -- only an actual, compliant notice does that. This corrects a natural but imprecise assumption: the statute does not set a single symmetrical '60-day notice period.' The required advance notice must be given at least 60 days before the exercise, but the defined 'notice period' itself runs only 59 days from the day notice is given, and the required contest warning likewise refers to 59 days, not 60 -- so the advance-notice figure and the contest-window figure described in this clause are not the same number. expectedJSON.body: Even where an authorized fiduciary holds expanded distributive discretion sufficient to exercise the decanting power, the Act places specific limits on what the resulting second trust may do. In an exercise of the decanting power under this expanded-discretion authority, a second trust may not include as a current beneficiary a person who is not already a current beneficiary of the first trust (except as the statute separately allows), may not include as a presumptive remainder or successor beneficiary a person who does not already hold one of those categories of interest in the first trust (subject to the same exception), and may not reduce or eliminate a 'vested interest' -- a term the Act itself defines to include, among other things, a current and noncontingent right to a mandatory distribution of income or a set dollar amount or percentage, and a presently exercisable general power of appointment. This is a narrower, more specific protection than a generic rule against reducing 'a beneficiary's interest' in the abstract: it turns on whether the particular interest at stake qualifies as a current beneficiary interest, a presumptive remainder or successor interest, or a statutorily defined vested interest, and it operates differently from the separate 'substantially similar' protection that applies instead when a fiduciary is decanting under limited, rather than expanded, distributive discretion.

citations.quote: (c) Subject to Section 19513, in an exercise of the decanting power under this section, a second trust may not do any of the following:(1) Include as a current beneficiary a person that is not a current beneficiary of the first trust, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (d).(2) Include as a presumptive remainder beneficiary or successor beneficiary a person that is not a current beneficiary, presumptive remainder beneficiary, or successor beneficiary of the first trust, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (d).(3) Reduce or eliminate a vested interest.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's specific beneficiary protections under this Act -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, or about how any specific first trust's beneficiaries or interests should be categorized under this statute. This corrects a natural but imprecise assumption from a generic description of decanting statutes: California's statute does not flatly bar 'adding a new beneficiary' in every sense, and it does not use a single undifferentiated concept of 'a beneficiary's fixed income interest.' The restriction in subdivision (c) is limited to adding a person as a current beneficiary, or as a presumptive remainder or successor beneficiary, who does not already hold an equivalent category of interest in the first trust (itself subject to an exception in subdivision (d), which this document does not independently quote or address, for new or modified powers of appointment in favor of existing beneficiaries), and the protection against reduction turns on the statute's own defined term 'vested interest' -- a term this document does not exhaustively quote in full -- rather than on every fixed or scheduled payment a beneficiary might expect. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 19511(c); no additional independent source was sought for this, and it was fetched as part of the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) described in this document's other clauses, twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times.

expectedJSON.body: The Act separately restricts decanting where a first trust holds a charitable interest or property whose tax treatment depends on specific terms. If a first trust contains a charitable interest, the second trust or trusts may not diminish that charitable interest, may not diminish the interest of an identified charitable organization that holds it, may not alter any charitable purpose stated in the first trust instrument, and may not alter any condition or restriction related to that charitable interest. Independently, a set of tax-qualification protections applies across a list of specific tax provisions the statute itself enumerates -- for example, if a first trust contains property that qualified, or would have qualified, for a marital deduction for gift or estate tax purposes, the second trust instrument may not include or omit a term that would have prevented that qualification, or reduced the deduction, under the same provision that let the original transfer qualify. The statute applies a parallel rule to several other tax-sensitive attributes it separately lists, including charitable-deduction qualification, the gift-tax annual exclusion, S-corporation shareholder eligibility, generation-skipping-transfer zero-inclusion-ratio status, and minimum-distribution treatment of retirement-plan property; the statute also gives a settlor, specifically, the right to object in a signed writing during the notice period where decanting would change whether the settlor retains the power to cause a trust to cease being a 'grantor trust' for income tax purposes.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 19514(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the restrictions on decanting a first trust that contains a charitable interest
citations.quote: (c) If a first trust contains a charitable interest, the second trust or trusts may not do any of the following:(1) Diminish the charitable interest.(2) Diminish the interest of an identified charitable organization that holds the charitable interest.(3) Alter any charitable purpose stated in the first trust instrument.(4) Alter any condition or restriction related to the charitable interest.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 19519(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: preservation of marital-deduction qualification as a representative tax-sensitive limitation
citations.quote: (1) If a first trust contains property that qualified, or would have qualified but for provisions of this part other than this section, for a marital deduction for purposes of the gift or estate tax under the Internal Revenue Code or a state gift, estate, or inheritance tax, the second trust instrument shall not include or omit any term that, if included in or omitted from the trust instrument for the trust to which the property was transferred, would have prevented the transfer from qualifying for the deduction, or would have reduced the amount of the deduction, under the same provisions of the Internal Revenue Code or state law under which the transfer qualified.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 19519(b)(10) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a settlor's right to object to a decanting that would change grantor-trust status
citations.quote: (10) An authorized fiduciary may not exercise the decanting power if a settlor objects in a signed writing delivered to the fiduciary within the notice period and either of the following conditions is satisfied:(A) The first trust and a second trust are both grantor trusts, in whole or in part, the first trust grants the settlor or another person the power to cause the first trust to cease to be a grantor trust, and the second trust does not grant an equivalent power to the settlor or other person.
